chapters.title: Soul and Body, Wished Together
chapters.teaser: John's famous greeting to Gaius ties physical health to a soul that's already thriving.
body: "Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth" (v.2) is a warm, ordinary ancient greeting-wish, elevated by its second half. The comparison assumes something already established: Gaius's soul is prospering, evidenced by the report that follows of his faithful walk and generous hospitality (v.3-6).

This verse has sometimes been stretched into a promise of guaranteed material wealth for the faithful, detached from its context. Read plainly, it's simply a personal letter's opening kindness — but a kindness that still assumes spiritual health, love of the truth, and a life well-lived are the deeper, prior reality that any wish for outward wellbeing rests on.

chapters.title: Hospitality as Gospel Partnership
chapters.teaser: Gaius is praised for supporting traveling missionaries who took nothing from outsiders.
body: "Thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers" (v.5) commends Gaius for hosting itinerant workers he'd likely never met before — a real risk and real cost in the ancient world, where travel meant depending on local believers for food, lodging, and safe passage.

Verse 7 explains why their support mattered so much: these workers went out "for his name's sake, taking nothing of the Gentiles" — refusing pagan patronage that might compromise or obligate them. That left local Christian hospitality as their only viable support system. "We therefore ought to receive such," John concludes, "that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth" (v.8) — hosting a traveling teacher made the host an active partner in the mission itself, not just a passive well-wisher.

chapters.title: Diotrephes and the Politics of a Local Church
chapters.teaser: A named troublemaker gives a rare, candid glimpse into conflict inside an early congregation.
body: "Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not" (v.9) is startlingly specific for such a short letter — a real name, a real grievance, aimed at someone actively undermining John's own authority and instructions. This isn't abstract false teaching like the antichrists of 1 and 2 John; it's a leadership power struggle.

The charges are concrete: Diotrephes spreads "malicious words," refuses to welcome traveling believers himself, and even "casteth them out of the church" when others try to host them (v.10). It's a sobering reminder that the early church's dangers weren't only theological error from outsiders — ordinary ambition and control inside a congregation could just as easily choke out hospitality and truth.

chapters.title: Follow What Is Good
chapters.teaser: John reduces the letter's tension to a simple moral principle: imitate good, not evil.
body: "Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good. He that doeth good is of God: but he that doeth evil hath not seen God" (v.11) arrives right after the account of Diotrephes, functioning as the letter's ethical center of gravity. It's addressed to Gaius, but clearly meant as a broader test — a way of sorting real spiritual sight from its absence, tying back to the visible, practical love this whole small book keeps insisting on.

The principle is simple almost to the point of understatement, but that's the point: after cataloguing hospitality, mission support, and one leader's petty tyranny, John doesn't offer a complicated theological resolution. He offers a rule anyone can apply immediately — watch what a person actually does.

chapters.title: Demetrius, the Counter-Example
chapters.teaser: A second named figure closes the letter as the positive mirror image of Diotrephes.
body: "Demetrius hath good report of all men, and of the truth itself: yea, and we also bear record; and ye know that our record is true" (v.12) is placed deliberately right after the warning about Diotrephes — one man loving preeminence and excluding others, the other apparently commended by everyone, including truth itself personified as a witness.

The letter closes, almost identically to 2 John, preferring presence to paper: "I had many things to write, but I will not with ink and pen write unto thee: but I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face" (v.13-14). Even in a letter partly about conflict and correction, the last word is peace, friendship, and the hope of a real reunion — a fittingly personal close to the most personal letter in the New Testament.
